title: Incentive and Goal Reform
author: James Robinson
summary: James Robinson asks why education reforms such as high expectations, school choice and the science of reading never seem to scale, and answers that incentives and goals deserve more attention than courage or politics alone. After attending a Vanderbilt discussion where Roland Fryer said real change requires courage, he looked at the K-12 economy and found that student gaps pay consultants, curriculum vendors and service providers well. He offers five concrete reforms: assessments that test knowledge, charter authorizers who judge the learning science behind an applicant's model, state accountability that rewards growth only until proficiency, pay and training that treat new teachers as not ready on day one, and replacing consultants with well-paid fellows who solve one big problem and publish. The piece is brief but practical, framed as an invitation for academics to explore incentive design in K-12.
points: Reform ideas fail to scale partly because the K-12 economy profits from persistent gaps, so incentives rather than courage may be the binding constraint.
Redesigning assessments to require knowledge may be higher leverage than lobbying districts to adopt knowledge-rich curriculum first.
Charter authorizers should evaluate the learning science behind a school's design, not just finances and warmth.
Growth measures should drive recognition only for schools below the bar; above it, proficiency should be what gets paid and rewarded.
Hire fellows to solve one big problem and publish the results, rather than retaining consultants who gain from recurring work.
quotes: While there are pockets where all of the above is going well– none of it seems to scale. The ideas are just talk.
Unfortunately I couldn’t find a good answer. Depressingly, student gaps pay the employees and service providers very well.

Many writers are focused on districts and states adopting high-quality knowledge-based curriculum. While that is important, the highest leverage move may be to first re-design the assessments so that they require knowledge– then districts and schools will really need to implement knowledge-based curriculum.
Applying to open a school shouldn’t be just about finance and warmth– but effectiveness of design. No more innovative nature and driftwood schools please.

But what if we only recognized and incentivized academic growth until the school achieves above the state average? After reaching that milestone, schools would only be recognized and incentivized for proficiency.
Plan for new teachers not to be prepared to teach on day 1. If the teacher goes from a K12 education into a teaching program, there will likely be content gaps.
Traditional consultants don’t have any skin in the game. Effective solutions and closing gaps is a loss of recurring profits.
